logreg: Logistic Regression cannot memorise individual trips, yet it still shows a +3.7 pp train-vs-CV gap. That gap therefore measures how much easier the 20 sampled training trips are than the average held-out trip; it is not overfitting. We use it as the reference gap for the other models. Its CV Top-1 (0.892) is about 1 pp below the tree ensembles, which is mild underfitting: the linear boundary cannot combine heading agreement with speed or distance. Its probabilities are still well calibrated (CV log loss 0.108).
gnb: Gaussian NB has the lowest accuracy on every split (CV Top-1 0.868, student-test 0.848) and a log loss about 6x worse than the other models (0.648 on student_test). This is underfitting from model bias, not variance. The train-vs-CV gap (+4.2 pp) is close to the logistic-regression reference. The independence assumption counts the correlated distance features several times, which makes the probabilities over-confident. That disqualifies it as an HMM emission model.
knn: KNN's train-vs-CV gap is +6.3 pp, 2.6 pp above the reference. Part of this is memorisation: training fixes inside its 200k-row subsample find themselves as neighbours. CV Top-1 (0.887) and student-test Top-1 (0.882) are below the trees, so it overfits locally and generalises worse. It is also about 15x slower at inference (about 1.35 s per trip) than every other model, which matters for the API.
rf: Random Forest has the best CV Macro F1 (0.9443 ± 0.0108) and the best CV log loss (0.0775), and the most stable folds (lowest std together with LR). Its train-vs-CV gap (+5.1 pp, 1.4 pp above the reference) shows slight overfitting, which bagging and min_samples_leaf = 5 keep under control. On student_test it falls 1.3 pp below LightGBM in Top-1 (0.901 vs 0.914), and the saved model is 87 MB.
hgb: HistGradientBoosting lands between logistic regression and the other ensembles (CV Top-1 0.895, student-test 0.906). Its train-vs-CV gap (+5.2 pp, about 1.5 pp above the reference) shows little overfitting. With only 300 iterations and 31 leaves it is slightly under-capacity compared with LightGBM. It was also the slowest model to cross-validate (about 47 s per fold).
lgbm: LightGBM has the best student-test Top-1 (0.914), Macro F1 (0.950) and log loss (0.072), and its CV Macro F1 (0.9435 ± 0.0116) is statistically tied with RF. Its train-vs-CV gap (+6.3 pp, 2.6 pp above the reference) is the largest among the trees. With 63 leaves, no L2 penalty and min_child_samples = 20 it overfits mildly, which made it the natural candidate for Bayesian tuning of the regularisation parameters (num_leaves, min_child_samples, reg_lambda, subsampling).
mlp: The MLP reaches CV Top-1 0.899 and student-test 0.899, between the linear models and the tree ensembles. Its train-vs-CV gap (+4.8 pp, about 1 pp above the logistic-regression reference) shows little overfitting: early stopping picked epoch 13 of 17, when the validation loss stopped improving (Figure 17). Validation loss stays below training loss because dropout is active only during training, and the 8 validation trips happen to be easier than average. Even with 2x128 + 128x64 learned weights it does not beat boosted trees on these engineered tabular features, and it took the longest to train (98 s on 4 threads).
_features: What the model actually uses. The three most important features by gain are dist_minus_min (how much farther a candidate is than the closest one), angle_diff_long (heading over ±5 fixes vs arc bearing) and ctx_mean_dist_minus_min (how well the neighbouring fixes fit this arc compared with the best candidate). Relative distance, direction and temporal context are exactly the three patterns found in the EDA. Absolute distance alone (dist) contributes almost nothing once the relative versions are present, and the time-gap features are rarely used because 94% of steps are 1 s.
_selection: Random Forest and LightGBM are statistically tied on CV Macro F1 (0.9443 ± 0.0108 vs 0.9435 ± 0.0116; the difference is far smaller than the fold standard deviation). LightGBM is clearly better on the held-out student_test trips: Top-1 0.914 vs 0.901, Macro F1 0.950 vs 0.942, and the lowest log loss of all models (0.072). Good probability quality matters because the probabilities become HMM emissions. LightGBM's model is also 30x smaller than the RF (2.8 MB vs 87 MB), and its overfitting (largest train-CV gap) is controllable with regularisation hyperparameters, which makes it the best candidate for Bayesian optimisation. Naive Bayes (poor calibration) and KNN (slow inference, about 1.35 s/trip) are unsuitable for the API. All seven models show the same fold ranking (fold 3 is hardest), so variance across folds comes from trip difficulty, not from model instability. Note: timings were measured while other experiments shared the CPU, so they are comparable within a model family but noisy across runs.
_tuning: Partly. On the optimised objective the tuned model is better: 5-fold CV Macro F1 0.9445 vs 0.9435, CV Top-1 0.9031 vs 0.9014, CV log loss 0.0774 vs 0.0822, and the fold standard deviation dropped from 0.0104 to 0.0095. The best configuration is more regularised: shallower trees (max_depth 6), far larger leaves (min_child_samples 188), row/column subsampling of about 0.57, and a lower learning rate (0.028) with more trees (467). This is consistent with the mild overfitting found for the untuned model. On the 10 student_test trips, tuned Top-1 is 0.4 pp lower (0.9097 vs 0.9142) and Macro F1 0.3 pp lower, while log loss is slightly better (0.0713 vs 0.0718). With only 10 test trips, a 0.4 pp change is within the trip-to-trip variation (classifier-only per-trip Top-1 ranges from 0.80 to 0.98), so we treat the two as equivalent on student_test. We kept the tuned model because it was selected on training data only (as required) and has the better-calibrated probabilities, which the HMM uses. The search surface is very flat: all 14 completed trials lie within 0.9437–0.9451 CV Macro F1. fANOVA attributes most of the variation to n_estimators (61%) and reg_lambda (19%). Computational cost: 25 trials in about 12.5 minutes of wall time on 14 CPU threads (11 trials stopped early by the pruner). The final fit takes about 10–15 s and inference stays in the tens of milliseconds per trip.
_hmm: Yes, clearly. On student_test, HMM decoding raises pooled Top-1 from 0.9097 to 0.9470 (+3.7 pp) and route continuity from 0.821 to 0.904. The largest effect is on the reconstructed route: arc-set precision rises from 0.690 to 0.965 (route F1 0.807 to 0.978), because the classifier-only route contains many isolated wrong arcs (parallel lanes, opposite-direction twins, side streets) that the transition model removes. Unbridged breaks drop from 88 to 3. At sequence level, 7/10 trips exceed 95% Top-1 after decoding vs 4/10 before. Every one of the 10 student_test trips improves (+1.7 to +6.5 pp, Table 8), with the largest gain on the hardest trip (00000077, 0.798 to 0.863). The classifier emission matters: a classic HMM with a distance-only Gaussian emission reaches only 0.9256, and on train its per-trip mean Top-1 (0.916) is clearly below classifier emissions (0.933). The best decoder uses α = 0.5, so the transition model gets relatively more weight. α = 0.5 is the edge of our grid, so smaller values could be explored. Where HMM did not help. On the 80 training trips (out-of-fold), HMM decoding lowered Top-1 on 4 trips, by at most 0.75 pp (00000097: 0.988 to 0.981, 00000044: 0.985 to 0.978, 00000089: 0.862 to 0.860, 00000005: 0.974 to 0.973). Three of these already had near-perfect classifier output and fast driving (median step 14–31 m). Here the β = 5 m transition penalty sometimes keeps the vehicle on the current arc for one fix too long at intersections, where the per-fix reference label is itself ambiguous. Trip 00000089 has four gaps longer than 60 s, a reference-route break and 1.5% candidate misses, so the decoder restarts without context and cannot recover arcs that are not candidates. The remaining errors after decoding are mostly opposite-direction twin arcs while the vehicle is stationary (heading undefined), and the transitions between consecutive arcs at intersections. Route continuity below 1.0 is expected with our strict definition: when a short arc is crossed between two 1 Hz fixes, the per-fix sequence skips it, even though build_route bridges it in the final route.
